content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a new methodology to create synthetic population data, down to the individual and family level, for a geographic region. The paper uses two synthetic data generation models, IPU and CTGAN, combined with geographic sampling and assignment heuristics to produce the population data. In addition to the proposed model, the paper also outlines some methods to evaluate the quality of the synthetic data, given comparable real data. Finally, the paper empirically demonstrated the utility of its proposed approach by applying its method to a real-world example (Mumbai, India) and with a salient use of the synthetic data, Agent-based modeling of disease spread dynamics.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper presents a relatively straightforward use of existing models to generate artificial, tabular data combined with some useful heuristics to deal with geographic data. The paper is also well-written and contains helpful images. The paper could present a moderately significant methodological contribution; however, some issues need to be addressed for it to be so.
The major weaknesses of the paper are in its contribution, reproducibility, and soundness.

-	The contribution of the paper seems somewhat trivial. While the problem the paper is attacking (the need to generate population data sets that preserve privacy and are accurate down to the person and family level) is certainly significant, the approach seems very incremental. More specifically, the method presented in the paper seems to be mostly just a rote combination of two other existing methods (i.e. IPU and CTGAN). Other than combining these methods, what is the real contribution of this paper in terms of the method presented?

-	For the reproducibility of the paper, it's not clear how to use the presented method with new data. Specifically, what types of data (i.e. continuous, categorical, etc.) go to which methods (i.e. IPU versus CTGAN)? Also, how much overlap in the data is required between the different pieces of the data? For example, how many individuals are present in IHDS Survey Data and the Census data such that you can link the data between these two inputs? The paper would benefit from providing some of these details, especially in figure 1, such that a new researcher knows how to plug their data correctly.

-	There are some issues with the soundness of the paper. First, for the ABM validation, what is the comparison of the ABM model run with the real data versus the synthetic data? Was it even possible to run the ABM with real data? If not, the ABM validation is really only a face validation only (i.e. the results of the infected individuals over time “look right”). Second, for the proposed model, it seems like the generation of categorical attributes, continuous attributes, and geographic attributes are all done independently of each other. So, what if any of these variables affect other variables, like the categorical variable of sex affecting the continuous variables of weight and height?

-	The presented metrics to validate the synthetic data are not novel. The paper presents the same techniques used in other papers for validating synthetic data – does the synthetic data have distributions that match given data distributions and do follow-on tasks perform roughly the same on the synthetic data as they do on real data. It would be good to see more innovation in this area. For example, is it possible to evaluate all possible marginal and joint distributions to produce a measure of goodness? Or, is it possible to get a measure of the robustness of generated data as more or less real data is available?

Some minor issues are:
-	For tables 1 and 2, please provide more description of what the numbers mean. What is KSTest of 0.94? Is that the p-score? What is 0.72 for Linear Regression? Is that the mean squared error? 

-	Also for the tests run for Table 2, a better measure might be to fit the same models multiple times on each data set (random and synthetic), with different random initializations, and then compare the two data sets' models outputs and parameter values statistically. 

-	Since the IPU and CTGAN procedures are so important to the paper, it might be worth providing some more description of them in section 3.1 for clarity and maybe to shore up the contribution of the paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The clarity of the paper is generally high. The paper does, however, need to provide some more details for reproducibility and, probably, for novelty (see previous comments). The paper also needs to address its issues with the soundness of its procedure and the validation scheme to be a more quality paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: While the paper is well-written and is attacking a significant problem, the lack of contribution and issues with its validation make this paper a reject in its current format. Also, it would be good for the paper to be modified in such a way that the method could be easily adapted to new use cases. I believe that if the paper were to address these issues, it could present a very useful method and possibly some novel contributions, like better measures of synthetic, population data.

content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 5XDr
content.comment:
Thank you for the detailed feedback and suggestions. 

For 2nd point under strength and weaknesses, the Census of India data is only summary statistics for various demographic and socio-economic attributes. Census of India does not release micro-data for public use on easily accessible platforms. Our method uses micro data from IHDS as input to IPU and generates population to match the summary statistics from Census. There are no exact matches done between these two datasets. 

For 3rd point under strength and weaknesses, as ABM needs population scale data, the real data (which is just a sample survey) cannot be used for this purpose. So, there is no comparison between ABM with real vs ABM with synthetic population. Also, we do not assume independence of columns- e.g., the columns for height and weight are conditionally generated based on age and sex column. 

Thank you for the 4th point- we are actively working in that direction to add more meaningful verification metrics, including a longer term primary survey.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper designs a hybrid framework that can combine data from multiple real-world surveys to produce a real-scale synthetic population of humans. Specifically, the proposed framework can generate “fake” people with the realistic distribution of family structures and various individual attributes covering demographic, socioeconomic, health, and geolocation factors. It combines Iterative Proportional Updating and Conditional Tabular GAN to generate families and individuals and their related metadata. Further, reject sampling is used to sample geolocation points within a city’s boundaries according to population density distribution. Both machine learning and statistical metrics are used to evaluate the quality of generated population data, along with a case study on agent-based modeling of infectious diseases in India.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1.    The research problem of generating a synthetic population is generally well-motivated, with both research value and application potential.
2.    A case study on epidemic control is provided, which is an important and promising application direction for such a synthetic data generation approach.
3.    The paper is well-written and easy to follow.


Weaknesses:

1. The currently presented evaluations are not enough to support the validity of the proposed generation framework. More specifically, 
    - No evaluation of family structures is provided.
    - Table 1 only reports average statistical test scores instead of detailed values on each attribute.
    - Details of the machine learning model test are also missing.
    - Evaluations in Figure 2-5 are based on a visualization angle and do not have quantitative metrics.
2. One important aspect of possible privacy leakage in synthetic data generation has not been studied.
3. The authors should summarize the innovation points of the proposed framework. Currently, it seems like a hybrid combination of several generation approaches.
4.  Some claims should be justified by providing more evidence. 
    - The proposed framework can synthesize populations with a list of attributes for which no survey has been conducted. 
    - The assumption that the workplace distribution follows the population density distribution.
    - The calculation of the probability of the individual being assigned the external location.
5.  The validity of using a synthetic population for agent-based simulation should also be evaluated.
6.  Some small typos. For example, on page 2, “which uses a hybrid 1 of IPU and CTGAN to take advantage”.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
There exists a large room for improving clarity. For example,
- Figure 1 should be put on page 3.
- Why introduce graph neural networks in the introduction? “with the advent of graph neural networks and the growing complexity of Agent-based models,”
- Some references should be cited using the format of the parenthetical citation, like “between a given individual's household and the external location Ministry of Education (2019).”

The novelty is limited even for an application paper.

As for reproducibility, the authors have provided the source code and datasets.
content.summary_of_the_review: Given the listed weaknesses and other comments on clarity and novelty, I stand for the rejection for this paper.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper6493 by Reviewer ZZns

content.title: Response to Reviewer ZZns
content.comment:
Thank you so much for your valuable feedback. 

For point no 2 in weaknesses, one source, IHDS-II is nominally anonymous data. Additionally, IHDS-II replaces village names with a unique code in their data to prevent re-identification. Another source we use is Census of India, which is the summary statistics for various attributes across the country. We take the reviewer's point regarding privacy leakage in our hybrid model as we start including private data; each such data source would indeed need to be checked.

For point no 4 in weaknesses: 
We stress that for population attributes, we only model and generate columns which are already present in the sample survey data. Even the geolocation assignments for houses, workplaces, schools and public places are confined to the geography of the surveyed administrative area. Another concern raised is about the assumption that the workplace distribution follows the population density distribution- we have mentioned two points in para 2 of section 3.2. First, this assumption is not valid in cities where people live in outer sub-urban areas and work closer to the city center. Second, given the lack of appropriate dataset for workplace distribution, we resorted to this assumption. Once we have relevant information, we would refine our approach to workplace assignment.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a novel hybrid framework that combines data from multiple sources (survey data) and generates a country-scale synthetic-population which can be used for modelling disease spread. The framework combines existing methods, Iterative Proportional Updating (IPU) and Conditional Tabular GAN (CTGAN) to generate base population and additional columns corresponding to individual level attributes. The paper presents statistical metrics to evaluate the quality of the synthetic population generated by the proposed framework. Experimental results show that the synthetic population is a realistic simulation of the population.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
1. A novel framework for generating synthetic population as needed for a particular downstream task is proposed.
2. Metrics are proposed to evaluate the framework.
3. Experiments sections shows steps in generating synthetic population for the Mumbai City District with over 3M population.

Weaknesses
1. The synthetic population is not compared to those generated by existing methods. This could provide clear understanding on where this synthetic population performs better (or worse) than existing methods. 
2. The methodology related contributions are incremental.

1. The paper is well written and easy to follow.
2. The code to reproduce the results is provided.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 1aX9
content.comment:
Thank you for so much for the review and helpful suggestions. We have mentioned in Section 2, Related Work, about existing methods and their deficiencies, which our method tries to mitigate. Our method to generate the synthetic population is a novel hybrid of techniques applied at a scale (both population size and number of attributes) many orders of magnitude beyond any previous attempts. Specifically, we do not ``scale'' at all - we produce a synthetic population at the same size as the real one. For this reason, comparing our synthetic population with synthetic populations generated by other methods is not meaningful.

We had, of course, initially tried to just use basic methods such as CTGAN to do everything. This did not work. There have been very few attempts to generate synthetic populations of any reasonable size in the first place. As such, we hope our method will be of use to researchers who need such a dataset and simulation system.
